title: Trump to Nominate Doctor Who Has Publicly Supported Vaccines as C.D.C. Director
summary:
President Trump has nominated Dr. Erica Schwartz, a physician and vaccine supporter, to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, signaling a shift away from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s vaccine skepticism ahead of midterm elections. Dr. Schwartz, who holds degrees in biomedical engineering, medicine, public health, and law, served as deputy surgeon general during Trump's first term and is considered a highly qualified, traditional choice. She has publicly praised vaccines while also supporting healthy diet and exercise initiatives aligned with Kennedy's focus on chronic diseases.

If confirmed by the Senate, Dr. Schwartz would become the agency's fourth director in just over a year, inheriting challenges including employee morale following widespread layoffs, a headquarters shooting, and declining public trust. The administration also announced additional appointments, replacing political appointees more closely aligned with Kennedy's vaccine skepticism. Some public health experts welcomed her credentials, while Kennedy allies criticized her past enforcement of vaccine mandates. The CDC has lacked permanent leadership for most of Trump's second term after previous nominees faced opposition over vaccine positions.

title: The contradiction at the heart of Republicans’ embrace of psychedelics
summary:
President Trump signed an executive order Saturday to expand psychedelic access for mental health treatment, with podcaster Joe Rogan present. Trump joins other Republicans, including former Texas Governor Rick Perry, in championing psychedelics like ibogaine for treating trauma and addiction in veterans. GOP lawmakers have introduced legislation directing federal agencies to study compounds including ibogaine, MDMA, and psilocybin, while Texas has allocated tens of millions for psychedelic research.

Two professionals with decades of experience in addiction and psychiatric care acknowledge that psychedelics show promise but argue they cannot work in isolation. Research indicates the strongest predictors of sustained recovery are social support and recovery capital, including stable housing, employment, healthcare access, and supportive relationships. Studies on mental illness and trauma recovery point to similar factors.

The authors identify a contradiction: many politicians promoting psychedelics have supported budget cuts exceeding $1 trillion to programs funding addiction treatment, mental healthcare, housing stability, and economic security through legislation like the "One Big Beautiful Bill." They argue that removing these material conditions undermines recovery regardless of available pharmacological tools, particularly for veterans facing housing insecurity and understaffed mental health systems after treatment.

title: Nebraska begins Medicaid work requirements ahead of federal deadline
summary:
Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services began implementing work requirements for certain Medicaid recipients on May 1, making it the first state to enact the policy before a federal deadline. The requirements apply to able-bodied adults ages 19 to 64 covered under Medicaid expansion and stem from federal legislation H.R. 1, which mandates states adopt such policies by January 1, 2027. Enrollees must complete at least 80 hours monthly of qualifying activities including employment, education, job training, or volunteering, or meet an equivalent income threshold. New applicants must comply immediately, while current enrollees will be evaluated at their next renewal. Exemptions apply to people with disabilities, pregnant individuals, and those facing temporary hardships.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates 9.9 to 14.9 million people could lose coverage by 2034 due to administrative challenges and reporting requirements. The Congressional Budget Office projects work requirements could contribute to 16 million additional uninsured people by 2034. Research indicates such requirements typically do not increase employment but lead to coverage losses and delayed care. Most states plan to implement requirements closer to the 2027 deadline, with many facing logistical challenges regarding verification and system updates.

title: RFK Jr. Wants to Wean Some Americans Off Antidepressants
summary:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced initiatives aimed at helping Americans reduce psychiatric medication use, particularly antidepressants. Speaking at a Make America Healthy Again Institute event, Kennedy stated that many patients lack clear understanding of medication risks and withdrawal processes. The Department of Health and Human Services will issue guidance encouraging non-drug mental health interventions, while the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will allow doctors to bill for services related to tapering patients off psychiatric medications.

Antidepressants are widely prescribed in the U.S., with 16.6% of adults currently taking them according to a 2025 survey. While these medications can be critical interventions, concerns have grown about withdrawal difficulties. Kennedy emphasized that patients should not stop medications without proper guidance, though he compared antidepressant withdrawal to heroin addiction based on personal experience.

Patient advocacy groups have petitioned the FDA for stronger warnings about prolonged withdrawal symptoms, noting that rapid tapering can cause severe effects lasting months or years. A 2022 study found only 15% of people with major depression experienced substantial benefits beyond placebo effects. The median treatment duration is five years, despite limited evidence supporting long-term effectiveness. Antidepressant use has risen particularly among young women.

title: Food stamp work rules don't increase employment, researchers say
summary:
A mobile food pantry in Mingo County, West Virginia, serves dozens of residents struggling with food insecurity amid new federal SNAP work requirements. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act now requires able-bodied adults aged 18-64 without dependents to work, volunteer, or participate in job training at least 80 hours monthly to maintain benefits beyond three months every three years. The age limit was previously 54, and the law eliminated exemptions for veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster youth.

Lilly Hall, 59, whose husband has cancer and whose household survives on $1,500 monthly Social Security, found unpaid restaurant work to preserve her benefits. Research from the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy found work requirements don't reduce unemployment or increase labor participation. In Mingo County, where a quarter of residents live in poverty and jobs are scarce following coal industry decline, researchers identified significant employment barriers including lack of transportation, internet access, and documentation.

Beginning in October, states will assume 75% of SNAP administrative costs, with additional penalties for error rates starting in 2027. Analysts estimate Kentucky could lose 114,000 recipients and worry some states may discontinue SNAP entirely. Meanwhile, local food pantries continue serving communities, distributing hundreds of boxes monthly.

title: Why Congress failed to reach an Obamacare deal
summary: Pennsylvania Republican Brian Fitzpatrick led a bipartisan effort last fall to extend enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies before their December 31 expiration, warning that failure would cause insurance premiums to soar for 24 million Americans. The subsidies, enacted by Democrats in 2021 and extended in 2022, were not made permanent during the Biden administration. Despite warnings from states, hospitals, and employers about cascading effects, Congress delayed action. A Congressional Budget Office report estimated nearly four million Americans would lose coverage over a decade without the subsidies, while extending them would cost $350 billion. Negotiations became entangled with abortion policy, specifically the Hyde Amendment restricting federal funding for abortion. Republicans cited concerns about fraud and ideological opposition to Obamacare, while Democrats made the extension a priority. A 43-day government shutdown from October to November further complicated matters. Senate bipartisan talks collapsed in February over Hyde Amendment language proposed for health savings accounts. The White House remained largely uninvolved throughout negotiations. Without the subsidies, median premiums jumped 18 percent, with some couples facing increases exceeding 500 percent. ACA enrollment declined by over one million people for 2026.

title: Federal judge halts RFK Jr.'s changes to children's vaccine policies
summary: A federal judge in Boston has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's vaccine policy changes, ruling that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. improperly replaced members of a key CDC advisory committee. U.S. District Court Judge Brian Murphy halted decisions made by the reconstituted Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which had recommended reducing federally recommended childhood vaccinations. The judge determined that Kennedy's actions were arbitrary and capricious, disregarding established scientific processes for developing vaccine policies. Kennedy had fired the committee's previous members in June 2025 and appointed 13 new members, many of whom had criticized vaccines. The reconstituted committee had issued controversial recommendations, including advising against universal hepatitis B vaccination for newborns. The ruling forced postponement of a committee meeting scheduled for later in the week that was expected to address COVID-19 vaccines and potentially revise federal vaccine policy formulation. The American Academy of Pediatrics and other health groups that filed the lawsuit praised the decision. The Department of Health and Human Services announced plans to appeal, with a spokesman stating the administration expects the ruling to be overturned.

title: Seniors Paid Billions in Extra Premiums Due to Alleged Medicare Overpayments
summary:
A congressional committee report found that Medicare Part B premiums for seniors were approximately 10% higher in 2025, costing an average of $212 more annually, due to alleged overpayments to Medicare Advantage plans. The Joint Economic Committee attributed these increased costs to controversial insurer practices, including adding diagnoses to trigger higher reimbursements. The report, prepared by the committee's Republican majority staff, estimated overpayments totaled $13.4 billion, affecting both Medicare Advantage enrollees and traditional Medicare beneficiaries. Higher-income recipients faced additional costs up to $682 annually.

The committee based its calculations on findings from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, which estimated Medicare Advantage plans cost roughly 20% more than traditional Medicare for covering the same individuals. This difference stems from insurers documenting additional diagnoses and enrolling healthier-than-average recipients. The health insurance industry trade group AHIP disputed the findings, calling the data and methodology fundamentally flawed. Medicare administrator Mehmet Oz stated that while insurers may not be as overpaid as reported, the payment system has created problematic incentives requiring rule changes. The Medicare agency recently proposed removing certain tools insurers use to increase payments.

title: FDA backs away from RFK Jr.’s claims about drug’s promise for autism patients
summary:
The Food and Drug Administration announced Monday it lacks sufficient evidence to support using leucovorin to treat autism in children, reversing earlier optimistic statements from FDA Commissioner Marty Makary and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In September, Makary claimed the drug could help "hundreds of thousands" of children with autism, citing a study showing improvement in two-thirds of children with autism and folate deficiency. However, that study was recently retracted due to errors.

Instead, the FDA approved leucovorin Tuesday for treating an ultra-rare disease affecting fewer than one in a million people, caused by cerebral folate transport deficiency related to the CFD-FOLR1 gene. This condition can cause severe developmental delays, movement disorders, and seizures. Makary stated the approval "may benefit some individuals" with this deficiency who have developmental delays with autistic features.

Senior FDA officials emphasized the agency remains committed to approving products based on established evidentiary standards, which were met for the rare disease but not for autism broadly. The agency remains open to future studies examining leucovorin's use for autism. Officials noted the drug is not currently in shortage, though demand increased following September's announcements.

title: Federal court blocks Kennedy’s vaccine changes, invalidates vaccine advisory panel
summary:
A federal judge has blocked Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s modifications to vaccine policy, including changes to childhood immunization recommendations and the restructuring of a key advisory committee. U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy granted a preliminary injunction requested by the American Academy of Pediatrics, finding that the reconstitution of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act. The judge determined that the CDC's decision to bypass the committee when altering the childhood immunization schedule was both procedurally flawed and an abandonment of technical expertise.

Kennedy had dismissed all seventeen ACIP members in June, subsequently appointing vaccine skeptics and critics. The reconstituted committee voted to eliminate recommendations for hepatitis B vaccines at birth, delay certain combination vaccines, and modify COVID-19 vaccine guidance. Judge Murphy found significant expertise gaps among new appointees, noting that only six of fifteen members possessed meaningful vaccine experience, while six others appeared to lack relevant qualifications entirely. The Department of Health and Human Services announced plans to appeal the decision. While the judge declined to block upcoming meetings, he noted they are effectively canceled due to the invalidated appointments.

title: Anti-Abortion March Brings Thousands to D.C., and a Sense of Frustration
summary:
At the annual March for Life, anti-abortion activists expressed frustration with the pace of progress under President Trump's second term, despite having allies in key positions. Vice President JD Vance acknowledged their concerns, stating "I hear you and I understand" regarding fears that insufficient progress has been made. While activists credit Trump for appointing Supreme Court justices who overturned Roe v. Wade, recent actions have disappointed them, including FDA approval of generic mifepristone and Trump's comments about flexibility on the Hyde Amendment, which prohibits federal funding for abortion.

The administration announced several policy changes at a White House briefing, including reinstating a ban on fetal tissue research and expanding restrictions on international organizations that perform abortions. However, anti-abortion leaders view these as incremental steps. Marjorie Dannenfelser of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America stated the administration "has not moved when it absolutely could move."

Some activists, particularly from states like Texas with strict abortion bans, find the federal situation "dire" compared to state-level advances. They continue pressing for enforcement of the Comstock Act to restrict mailing abortion pills, though such action appears unlikely currently.

title: Supreme Court restores abortion pill access — for now
summary:
Justice Samuel Alito has temporarily restored access to the abortion drug mifepristone after a federal appeals court limited its availability. The brief order, issued Monday, puts on hold a 5th Circuit Court of Appeals decision that restricted how patients could obtain the medication. Alito's order remains in effect through May 11, allowing the full Supreme Court time to consider requests from mifepristone manufacturers Danco and GenBioPro to maintain the stay while deciding whether to take up the case.

The pharmaceutical companies argued that Supreme Court intervention is necessary to prevent "regulatory chaos," emphasizing the importance of FDA scientific judgment in drug regulation. The temporary restoration allows doctors in states with abortion protections to prescribe mifepristone via telehealth and send it by mail, a common method for patients to circumvent state bans. Louisiana has until May 7 to respond to the emergency appeals.

Following the 5th Circuit ruling, some telehealth abortion providers paused services or switched to prescribing only misoprostol, the second pill in the two-pill regimen, which can terminate pregnancies independently but has higher failure rates and more severe side effects. Anti-abortion activists expressed frustration with Alito's decision, while abortion rights advocates warned of confusion and fear among patients and providers.

title: RFK Jr. launches plan to address ‘overuse’ of psychiatric medications
summary:
US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a plan to address what he termed "overprescribing" of psychiatric medications, particularly among children, while promoting alternative treatments and medication discontinuation when appropriate. Speaking at a MAHA Institute summit on mental health, Kennedy emphasized patient autonomy, informed consent, and a shift toward prevention and holistic approaches to mental health care.

The announcement aligns with recent efforts by psychiatric professionals, including February guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology on appropriate medication discontinuation. While some psychiatry experts welcomed federal efforts to improve psychiatric healthcare, they expressed concerns about overemphasizing overprescribing while mental healthcare access remains inadequate.

Kennedy has previously claimed psychiatric medications, especially antidepressants, are overused and linked to violence, mass shootings, fetal risks, severe withdrawal, and harm to children. However, the FDA has deemed these medications generally safe and effective for treating depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, though some slight risks exist in certain situations.

Medical experts noted that both overprescribing and underprescribing are concerns across all medicine, emphasizing that psychiatric medications can be lifesaving when appropriately prescribed.

title: Fertility treatment given special emphasis as Trump Rx site goes live
summary: The Trump administration's TrumpRx drug discount program launched this month with coupons for 43 medications, including four fertility drugs used in IVF procedures. Experts view this as a limited attempt to fulfill Trump's 2024 campaign promise of universal IVF access. The program currently offers discounts primarily for fertility medications, weight loss drugs, and menopause treatments, with additional medications promised in coming months. However, fertility drug costs represent only 10 to 20 percent of total IVF expenses. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimates TrumpRx could save patients up to $2,200 per IVF cycle, while total out-of-pocket costs can reach $30,000 per cycle, with multiple cycles often necessary. The Heritage Foundation, whose Project 2025 agenda has influenced Trump administration policies, opposes IVF on religious grounds, arguing embryos are "sacred human beings." Some experts suggest this opposition has prevented more comprehensive IVF access expansion. The Heritage Foundation promotes "restorative reproductive medicine" as an alternative, though medical professionals question its scientific validity and effectiveness compared to established IVF procedures.

title: Trump urges GOP to be ‘flexible’ on Hyde Amendment, igniting backlash from pro-life allies
summary:
President Donald Trump's recent remarks urging Republican lawmakers to be "flexible" on the Hyde Amendment have drawn sharp criticism from pro-life groups and activists. During a House Republican retreat at the Trump-Kennedy Center, Trump suggested flexibility on the 1976 law that prohibits most federal funding for abortions, including through Medicaid, as lawmakers work on healthcare legislation to address expired Obamacare subsidies.

Pro-life organizations swiftly condemned the comments. Students for Life Action President Kristan Hawkins stated that healthcare plans prioritizing deals over saving lives "deserve to die, not children." SBA Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser called opposition to taxpayer-funded abortion a "bedrock principle" of the Republican Party, warning that abandoning Hyde could cost Republicans in upcoming elections. Senator James Lankford expressed confusion about Trump's statement, saying he is "not flexible on the value of every child's life."

The remarks contrast with Trump's executive order signed nearly a year ago enforcing Hyde Amendment restrictions and rescinding Biden-era policies that expanded abortion access. Some conservatives have previously criticized Trump for insufficient support of pro-life policies during his 2024 campaign.

title: Exclusive: U.S. and Iran closing in on one-page memo to end war, officials say
summary: The White House reports progress toward a one-page memorandum of understanding with Iran that would end current hostilities and establish a framework for nuclear negotiations. U.S. officials expect Iranian responses on key points within 48 hours, though no agreement has been finalized. The proposed deal includes an Iranian moratorium on nuclear enrichment, U.S. sanctions relief and release of frozen Iranian funds, and mutual lifting of restrictions on Strait of Hormuz transit. The memorandum would declare an end to regional war and initiate a 30-day negotiation period for detailed agreements. Negotiations are being conducted by Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with Iranian officials. Key provisions under discussion include a 12-15 year enrichment moratorium, Iranian commitments to never pursue nuclear weapons, enhanced UN inspections including snap visits, and potential removal of highly enriched uranium from Iran. Many terms would be contingent on reaching a final agreement. U.S. officials acknowledge divisions within Iranian leadership and express skepticism about reaching consensus. Secretary of State Marco Rubio emphasized the need for clear diplomatic solutions while questioning whether Iranian leaders would ultimately agree to terms.

title: What We Know About the Memo the U.S. and Iran Are Discussing
summary: The United States and Iran are collaborating with mediators to develop a one-page, 14-point memorandum of understanding that would establish parameters for a month-long negotiation period aimed at ending the conflict. Talks could potentially resume next week in Islamabad, Pakistan. For the first time, Iran has indicated willingness to discuss its nuclear program. The proposed framework includes provisions for Iran to reduce restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz while the U.S. would scale back its blockade of Iranian ports during the 30-day negotiation window. Both parties are considering the removal of some Iranian highly enriched uranium stockpiles to foreign locations, though Iran opposes transferring nuclear material to the United States. Several key issues remain unresolved, including the duration of any enrichment suspension, Iran's role in overseeing the strait, and the scope of sanctions relief. The negotiation period could be extended by mutual agreement if discussions advance. Iran's Foreign Ministry confirmed the proposal is under review. President Trump stated he agreed to pause U.S. naval escort operations in the strait to facilitate negotiations, while warning of resumed military action if Iran fails to reach an agreement.

title: Trump opens Hormuz under fire with ‘Project Freedom’ as Iran warns of attacks
summary: The United States has launched "Project Freedom," a military operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, deploying guided-missile destroyers, over 100 aircraft, and approximately 15,000 service members. U.S. Central Command reports two U.S.-flagged merchant vessels have successfully transited the waterway under a defensive umbrella, though Iranian officials have rejected these claims as baseless. During the operation, American forces intercepted Iranian cruise missiles and drones while destroying six Iranian attack boats targeting commercial shipping. President Trump warned that Iranian strikes on U.S. vessels would be met with overwhelming force, while Iranian commanders threatened to attack any foreign military presence entering the strait. The operation does not involve individual ship escorts but provides layered naval, air, and electronic warfare protection across a cleared transit pathway. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps denies any successful transits occurred and has warned foreign forces will be attacked. The strait carries roughly a quarter of global seaborne oil trade, making disruptions significant for world markets. Retired military analysts note limited independent evidence of resumed commercial shipping at scale, questioning mine-clearing efforts and the operation's long-term sustainability if Iranian attacks intensify.

title: UAE to leave OPEC amid Hormuz oil crisis, a blow to Saudi Arabia
summary: The United Arab Emirates announced Tuesday it will exit the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and OPEC+ effective May 1, marking a significant blow to the Saudi-led group's influence over global oil prices. UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei stated the decision reflects the country's long-term strategic vision and evolving energy profile amid ongoing turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz affecting supply dynamics. The departure follows years of reported tensions and disagreements with Saudi Arabia over production quotas, recently exacerbated by conflicts in Yemen involving UAE-backed and Saudi-backed forces. The UAE becomes the second Persian Gulf nation to leave OPEC after Qatar's 2019 exit, reducing core membership to eleven countries. As OPEC's third-largest oil producer, the UAE's withdrawal weakens the organization during a period of energy market volatility stemming from Iran-related conflicts and strait closures. The move comes as President Donald Trump has criticized OPEC's role in determining oil prices and urged lower prices at the 2025 World Economic Forum. Analysts suggest the decision signals UAE's commitment to economic diversification beyond oil into sectors like artificial intelligence, trade, and tourism.

title: Trump Tells Aides to Prepare for Extended Blockade of Iran
summary: President Trump has directed aides to prepare for an extended blockade of Iran, opting to continue economic pressure rather than resume bombing or withdraw from the conflict. In a Monday Situation Room meeting, Trump rejected Iran's three-step proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, viewing it as negotiating in bad faith. The blockade aims to force Iran to dismantle its nuclear program, with Trump demanding at minimum a 20-year suspension of nuclear enrichment. The strategy has reduced transits through the Strait of Hormuz and strained Iran's economy, but has also elevated gas prices and affected Trump's poll numbers ahead of midterm elections. U.S. officials report the conflict may end without either a nuclear deal or resumed warfare. Negotiations remain stalled, with Iran consulting Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei before presenting a modified proposal. The blockade commits U.S. forces to prolonged Middle East deployment without guaranteeing regime capitulation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio noted that internal Iranian power struggles between hard-liners and negotiators complicate diplomatic efforts. Experts suggest both sides believe time favors their position.

title: Trump calls Iran’s proposal ‘totally unacceptable’
summary:
President Trump rejected Iran's response to his administration's peace proposal on Sunday, calling it "TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE" on Truth Social. The Islamic Republic News Agency confirmed that Iranian negotiators had submitted their response earlier that day. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, along with his army chief and foreign minister, has been mediating discussions between Tehran and Washington.

According to multiple reports, the Trump administration's proposal would require Iran to halt uranium enrichment in exchange for sanctions relief, with both sides lifting restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian military has threatened transit through the waterway and laid mines since a conflict began February 28, while the U.S. Navy has blockaded Iranian ports since April 13.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Iran's response does not meet U.S. demands on uranium enrichment. Instead, Tehran proposed ending hostilities and gradually reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with nuclear issues to be negotiated over 30 days. Iran suggested diluting some enriched uranium and transferring the remainder to a third country, with provisions for its return if negotiations fail. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated Friday that Iran would "never bow to pressure."

title: Senate Republicans again reject resolution to rein in Trump's Iran war
summary:
The Republican-controlled Senate rejected a Democratic resolution on Wednesday that would have required U.S. forces to withdraw from the conflict with Iran unless Congress authorizes further military action. The measure failed 47-52, marking the fourth time this year the Senate has declined to limit the president's war powers in this conflict. Republicans expressed support for President Trump's leadership while citing Iran's nuclear capabilities and the stakes involved in withdrawal, though some showed growing concern about the war's duration.

Under the 1973 War Powers Act, Congress must declare war or authorize force within 60 days of a conflict's start, with a possible 30-day extension. That deadline approaches at month's end. Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski is discussing a resolution to authorize the conflict beyond the deadline, while Senators Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, and others indicated Congress should vote on military authorization if the war continues. Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested the administration needs an exit strategy, noting that an upcoming White House funding request could provide Congress leverage. Democrats, including Senator Tammy Duckworth and Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, maintain the war is illegal and unnecessary, vowing continued efforts to end it.

title: What has the U.S. war with Iran accomplished?
summary: President Trump's stated goals for the war with Iran—ending its nuclear program, destroying military capabilities, and achieving regime change—remain largely unmet after more than five weeks of fighting and a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire. While U.S. officials claim significant damage to Iran's military infrastructure, the government survived and continues functioning. Iran maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway it has closed to most shipping, causing global oil price increases and creating leverage in negotiations. Experts suggest the conflict may have strengthened Iran's motivation to develop nuclear weapons, particularly following the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, whose religious decree had previously constrained such efforts. His son Mojtaba, described as more hard-line, has assumed leadership. The war surprised U.S. Gulf allies, who faced Iranian attacks without prior warning from Washington. Analysts indicate the conflict has damaged American credibility with allies, disrupted global markets, and potentially positioned Iran more advantageously than before hostilities began, while failing to achieve meaningful policy changes in Tehran.

title: Advocates of a two-state solution realise time to act is now
summary:
UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced Tuesday that Britain would recognize a Palestinian state at the UN General Assembly in September if Israel fails to meet certain conditions. This decision reflects growing international momentum toward a two-state solution as moderate voices compete against extremist visions for Gaza and the West Bank's future.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has declared that re-establishing settlements in Gaza is now a "realistic work plan," while reports suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may begin annexing parts of Gaza if Hamas rejects his ceasefire terms. Smotrich also predicted formal Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank during the current government's term.

A conference in New York, co-chaired by France and Saudi Arabia, produced the New York Declaration outlining a path to a two-state solution. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas committed to holding elections within a year, while the plan calls for Hamas to end its Gaza rule and surrender weapons. The declaration proposes establishing a transitional administrative committee under the Palestinian Authority and deploying an international stabilization mission.

International patience with Netanyahu's approach appears exhausted, with only eight percent of US Democrats supporting Israel's strategy according to recent polling.

title: Biden's Warning Over Rafah Sharpens a Problem for Netanyahu
summary: President Biden's warning to halt weapons supplies has intensified pressure on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces competing demands from international cease-fire calls and domestic right-wing pressure to invade Rafah in southern Gaza. Netanyahu responded defiantly, stating Israel would "stand alone" if necessary and fight "with our fingernails" to defeat Hamas. Biden threatened to withhold American weapons, including heavy bombs and artillery shells, if Israel proceeds with major operations in Rafah, where approximately one million Palestinians are sheltering. The administration has already withheld 1,800 2,000-pound bombs and 1,700 500-pound bombs, marking the first time Biden has acknowledged U.S. weapons killed civilians in Gaza, where over 34,000 have died according to local authorities. Israeli officials expressed mixed reactions. Former defense official Amos Gilead warned losing U.S. support would be unforgivable, while military spokesman Daniel Hagari insisted Israel has sufficient munitions for planned operations. Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich vowed to continue regardless. Some analysts compared the crisis to past U.S.-Israel disputes, suggesting it may not represent an unprecedented rupture in relations.

title: U.S., Arab nations plan for postwar Gaza, timeline for Palestinian state
summary:
The Biden administration and Middle Eastern partners are developing a comprehensive peace plan for Israel and Palestine, potentially to be announced within weeks. The initiative includes a timeline for Palestinian statehood and depends on a proposed six-week cease-fire and hostage release currently being negotiated by the United States, Qatar, and Egypt. Planners hope to reach an agreement before Ramadan begins March 10.

Participants include Egypt, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Palestinian representatives, and the United States. The plan envisions West Bank settler withdrawals, a Palestinian capital in East Jerusalem, Gaza reconstruction, and security arrangements combining the West Bank and Gaza. Israel would receive security guarantees and normalization with Arab states.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shown no willingness to accept Hamas's hostage deal demands or support Palestinian statehood, maintaining Israel must retain security control west of the Jordan River. Concerns exist that an Israeli attack on Rafah could derail negotiations.

The proposal includes early U.S. recognition of a Palestinian state and formation of an interim Palestinian government. However, skeptics question whether current Israeli and Palestinian leadership can achieve transformative solutions, noting decades of failed peace attempts.

title: Trump, Iran are locked in high-stakes standoff as oil prices hit 4-year high
summary:
The United States and Iran remain locked in a standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, with both sides confident they can outlast the other despite mounting global economic costs. Iran has deployed mines and drones to halt shipping through the crucial waterway, while the U.S. maintains a blockade of Iranian ports. Oil prices have surged to $126 per barrel, levels not seen since 2022, and U.S. gas prices reached $4.30 per gallon, a nearly four-year high.

President Trump insists negotiations must address Iran's nuclear program before any deal to reopen the strait, stating he will maintain the blockade until Iran agrees never to possess nuclear weapons. Iran proposes separating the issues, offering to negotiate reopening the strait first while postponing nuclear discussions. After initial talks in Islamabad failed, Iranian officials report that hard-liners have gained influence, making concessions on uranium enrichment less likely than before.

International opposition to Iran's closure exists, but no countries have offered military assistance to the U.S. Both nations continue imposing economic costs on each other, with no clear path to resolution as maximalist demands from both sides persist.

title: The U.S.-backed Gaza aid plan has started operating. Why are so many humanitarian groups opposed to it?
summary:
The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, a U.S.-backed organization approved by Israel, has begun aid distribution operations in Gaza despite opposition from the United Nations and most humanitarian groups. The foundation aims to replace the U.N.-led aid distribution system that has operated since October 2023. The new mechanism uses a limited number of guarded distribution hubs where Palestinians must collect supplies, with four hubs currently being established near Israeli military positions, three in the sparsely populated far south.

The foundation's executive director, Jake Wood, resigned Sunday, citing concerns the organization would not be allowed to operate independently. GHF claims to have over $100 million in commitments from an unnamed European Union government and plans to serve more than one million Palestinians by week's end, though Gaza's population is approximately 2.3 million.

The U.N. and aid organizations reject the new system, arguing it violates humanitarian principles and could enable forced displacement. They note the plan provides below-standard caloric intake and cannot adequately serve Gaza's population. Israel supports the change, accusing Hamas of diverting aid, which U.N. agencies deny. Hamas authorities have warned Palestinians against using GHF services.

title: Gaza talks turn to key sticking points between Israel, Hamas
summary: Delegations from Israel and Hamas began indirect negotiations in Egypt on Monday regarding U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza war. The talks, held at Sharm El Sheikh with Egyptian, American, and Qatari intermediaries, address contentious issues including Israeli troop withdrawal and Hamas disarmament. Both sides have endorsed the plan's general principles, which call for a ceasefire, hostage release, and increased humanitarian aid to Gaza. Trump expressed optimism about reaching a lasting agreement and has urged Israel to suspend bombing during negotiations. Gaza health authorities reported 19 deaths from Israeli strikes in the past 24 hours, a reduction from recent weeks. Hamas outlined its position on hostage releases and withdrawal timelines while expressing concerns about Israel's commitment to a permanent ceasefire. The negotiations began near the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack that killed 1,200 Israelis and took 251 hostages. Israel's subsequent military campaign has killed over 67,000 Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza's 2.2 million residents. Key sticking points include the timeline for hostage returns and Hamas's refusal to disarm without ending Israeli occupation and establishing a Palestinian state.

title: What is Hamas and why is it fighting with Israel in Gaza?
summary:
Hamas is an armed Palestinian group and political movement that has controlled the Gaza Strip since 2007. Designated as a terrorist organization by the US, UK, Israel, and other nations, Hamas originated as a Muslim Brotherhood offshoot in 1987 and opposes Israel's existence on what it considers Palestinian land.

On October 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israel, killing approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. The group justified this as a response to decades of Israeli oppression, the Gaza blockade, and alleged threats to the al-Aqsa mosque. Israel responded with a massive military offensive that has killed over 67,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, according to Gaza's health ministry. The conflict severely weakened Hamas, with Israel claiming to have killed more than 17,000 of its estimated 30,000 fighters.

Hamas's leadership has been decimated during the war. Leader Ismail Haniyeh was assassinated in Tehran in July 2024, and his successor Yahya Sinwar was killed by Israeli forces in October 2024. The group is now led by a five-man council headed by Khalil al-Hayya.

In October 2025, a ceasefire brokered by President Trump resulted in the release of remaining Israeli hostages and nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners.

title: Justices seem inclined to revive Trump policy blocking migrants at border
summary:
The Supreme Court appeared inclined on Tuesday to allow the Trump administration to revive a policy enabling border agents to block migrants from entering the United States to seek asylum. The case concerns interpreting immigration laws stating that noncitizens who "arrive in" the country must be permitted to apply for asylum. Under the disputed "metering" policy, border officials intercepted migrants approaching U.S. ports of entry and turned them back before reaching American soil. The policy began on a small scale during the Obama administration and expanded significantly during Trump's first term.

Lower courts sided with migrants challenging the policy, ruling that officers must process asylum seekers attempting to enter the United States, not only those physically inside its borders. The Trump administration argues the policy is a critical tool for managing border surges and that migrants must be physically inside the United States to claim asylum rights. During arguments, conservative justices expressed skepticism about whether migrants can "arrive in" the country before crossing the border, while some justices questioned whether the government's interpretation might incentivize illegal border crossings. The Biden administration had previously rescinded the policy.

title: Supreme Court considers letting Trump administration revive restrictive immigration asylum policy
summary:
The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday regarding whether the Trump administration can reinstate "metering," an immigration policy that limited asylum applications at the U.S.-Mexico border. The practice, which is not currently in effect, allowed authorities to restrict the number of daily asylum seekers, creating waiting lists and makeshift camps in Mexico during Trump's first term. The administration argues metering remains a necessary tool for managing border capacity, used by both Democratic and Republican administrations. Conservative justices appeared receptive to this position, while others questioned whether the policy unfairly privileges illegal border crossers over those seeking legal entry.

The legal dispute centers on interpreting "arrive in" under the Immigration and Nationality Act. The Justice Department contends it applies only to those already in the United States, while immigration advocates argue anyone at a port of entry must be allowed to apply for asylum. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noted the difficulty of ruling on a hypothetical policy not currently implemented. Lower courts previously ruled metering violated migrants' constitutional rights. The case is among several immigration matters before the Court this term.

title: Trump administration separates thousands of migrant families in the US
summary:
President Trump's current immigration enforcement efforts are separating families in ways distinct from his first-term zero-tolerance policy. While the earlier approach separated over 5,000 children at the border, current operations are dividing families of mixed legal status already residing in the United States. Federal detention facilities held an average of more than 66,000 people in November, a record high, as authorities arrest parents and either detain them for extended periods or deport them while children remain in the country.

Three families illustrate these separations. Antonio Laverde, a Venezuelan asylum-seeker working in Miami, was arrested and eventually returned to Venezuela after three months' detention, while his wife and children, who obtained refugee status, remain in Florida. A Nicaraguan couple who fled political persecution saw the husband deported after failing a credible fear interview, leaving his pregnant wife under GPS monitoring with their children. Edgar, a Guatemalan construction worker living in South Florida for over twenty years, was detained on an old traffic warrant and deported, separating him from his partner and newborn son. Administration officials describe the enforcement as "unprecedented success" and plan to continue current operations.

title: Democrats divided over Biden’s immigration executive order
summary:
President Biden's executive order Tuesday limiting migrant crossings at the southern border has created significant divisions within the Democratic Party. The order blocks migrants' access to the asylum system when illegal crossings exceed 2,500 daily, following failed congressional attempts at bipartisan immigration reform. Republicans previously voted against a bipartisan bill combining asylum caps with enforcement funding, partly due to opposition from former president Donald Trump.

While some Democrats view the executive action as necessary political outreach to independent voters, many criticized Biden for allegedly caving to Republican demands and potentially alienating the Democratic base. Progressive lawmakers, including Representatives Pramila Jayapal and Ilhan Omar, argued the order abandons American values and ignores asylum laws. Moderate Democrats called it an overdue but insufficient step.

Immigration ranks as a top voter concern, with polling showing 52 percent favor Trump's handling of the issue versus 41 percent for Biden. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer acknowledged executive action is less preferable than legislation but better than inaction. Democrats remain divided on whether the order goes too far or not far enough, with broad agreement that congressional action would be most effective.

title: US appeals court lets Texas keep river barrier against border crossings
summary:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled Wednesday that Texas may maintain a 1,000-foot floating barrier of buoys in the Rio Grande, reversing a lower court's preliminary injunction. The decision represents a victory for Texas Governor Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton in their ongoing legal disputes with the Biden administration over border enforcement measures.

The full appeals court determined that a lower court erred in finding the barrier occupies navigable waters, a key issue in the Biden administration's lawsuit alleging Texas violated federal environmental law requiring approval before constructing obstructions in such areas. The barrier, consisting of wrecking ball-sized buoys placed in a shallow river section, is part of Operation Lone Star, Abbott's broader border security initiative.

The Biden administration has challenged various Texas border enforcement actions as unlawful intrusions on federal immigration authority. Texas also faces legal battles over razor-wire fencing and a state law authorizing arrest and deportation of illegal border crossers. Similar laws in Iowa and Oklahoma have been blocked pending litigation.

A trial in the barrier case is scheduled to begin next week. The Fifth Circuit has twelve Republican-appointed judges among its seventeen active members.

title: US border security: What could Biden, Congress and Texas do?
summary: President Joe Biden is exploring whether he has legal authority to block migrants at the U.S.-Mexico border after Republicans rejected bipartisan legislation that would have granted such powers. The issue has become a central concern for Americans ahead of the November 2024 election. While Congress is responsible for federal immigration laws, partisan gridlock has prevented major reform for decades. The executive branch handles enforcement but faces legal challenges to its actions. Texas has attempted to implement its own immigration law allowing state authorities to arrest suspected illegal immigrants, though this faces court challenges. Biden has requested $13.6 billion in additional border funding for more agents, asylum officers, and judges, and supported a bipartisan Senate bill to tighten asylum rules. Republicans opposed both measures, demanding Biden restore Trump-era policies like the "remain in Mexico" program and border wall construction. The Biden administration is now considering using legal statute 212(f), previously employed for Trump's travel ban, to act unilaterally. Republicans argue Biden should reinstate restrictive Trump policies and end new legal entry programs, while Democrats maintain Republicans are blocking solutions for political reasons.

title: On US-Mexico bridge, two sides of Biden border crackdown
summary:
A group of Venezuelan migrants was deported from the United States on Saturday under the Biden administration's new asylum restrictions implemented June 5, which fast-track deportations of those crossing illegally. The deportees passed other migrants waiting for legal entry interviews through CBP One, a mobile phone application that provides lawful port-of-entry access. Despite facing five-year entry bans, some deportees indicated they would attempt crossing again.

President Biden has strengthened border security measures as immigration becomes a central issue before the November 5 elections against Donald Trump. The restrictive asylum policy and increased Mexican enforcement appear to be reducing crossings, with daily apprehensions falling to their lowest levels since February 2021. However, shelters in Ciudad Juarez report a forty percent increase in migrants seeking accommodation, as the CBP One app has become the primary legal entry method.

Border crossing attempts through dangerous desert routes have increased, with migrant deaths nearly doubling this fiscal year. Border Patrol rescues have nearly tripled, with approximately one heat-related death occurring daily in the El Paso sector. Activists attribute increased fatalities to policies criminalizing asylum seekers, forcing them toward more hazardous crossing routes.

title: Where Trump and Harris stand on immigration and border security
summary:
Immigration has emerged as a central issue in the November election, with Republicans criticizing the Biden administration's handling of border security. After initially promising a more compassionate immigration approach, President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris faced challenges controlling the southern border. The administration has both restricted asylum access and created new legal pathways for migrants to enter the United States.

Harris recently outlined plans to further limit asylum claims and extend existing restrictions during her first border visit as the Democratic presidential nominee. She has emphasized her law enforcement background and supports the failed bipartisan Senate compromise that would have tightened asylum standards and increased border personnel. While endorsing comprehensive immigration reform and pathways to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, Harris has criticized former President Trump's family separation policies.

Trump has made immigration central to his campaign, promising the largest domestic deportation operation in U.S. history if reelected. He plans to use the National Guard and invoke the 1798 Alien Enemies Act for deportations, end Biden-era entry programs, and reinstate policies like Remain in Mexico. Trump also proposes ending birthright citizenship for children of undocumented parents and implementing ideological screening for immigrants.

title: Harris promises tougher immigration, fentanyl controls at border
summary:
Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris visited the U.S.-Mexico border in Douglas, Arizona, on Friday, her first border visit during her 2024 presidential campaign. She called for tighter asylum restrictions and pledged to prioritize stopping fentanyl from entering the United States. Harris outlined plans to address what she termed a "broken immigration system" while accusing Republican rival Donald Trump of stoking fear over immigration.

Approximately 7 million migrants have been arrested crossing the border illegally during the Biden administration, a record high that has drawn Republican criticism. Harris proposed more punitive measures for illegal border crossings, including five-year re-entry bars and increased criminal charges for repeat violators. She also advocated for barring asylum requests from those who cross illegally outside legal entry points.

While emphasizing border security, Harris said she would pursue a "humane" immigration program, including a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers. She pledged to revive a bipartisan border security bill that failed in February after Trump urged Republicans to reject it. The legislation would add border personnel, asylum officers, and immigration judges.

Harris also committed to targeting the global fentanyl supply chain and doubling funding for prosecuting transnational criminal organizations.

title: Trump escalates harsh rhetoric against immigrants, Harris
summary:
Donald Trump delivered a speech in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, on Saturday focused heavily on immigration and border security, using harsh language to describe undocumented immigrants who have committed crimes. The Republican presidential candidate called them "monsters," "stone-cold killers," and "vile animals," while also directing personal attacks at Democratic opponent Kamala Harris, calling her "mentally impaired" and "mentally disabled." Trump blamed Harris and President Joe Biden for allowing undocumented immigrants into the country and accused some migrants of wanting to commit violent crimes against Americans.

The speech came after Harris visited the U.S.-Mexico border for the first time in her 2024 campaign, where she outlined plans to address immigration issues and accused Trump of "fanning the flames of fear and division." According to government data, approximately seven million migrants have been arrested crossing the border illegally during Biden's administration, a record high that has drawn Republican criticism.

Harris spokesperson Sarafina Chitika responded that Trump offered "nothing inspiring" but "just darkness." Studies generally show no evidence that immigrants commit crimes at higher rates than native-born Americans, though some families of crime victims have supported Trump's focus on the issue.

title: Democratic mayors face withering attacks on ‘sanctuary city’ policies
summary:
Four Democratic mayors from Boston, Chicago, Denver, and New York testified before a Republican-majority House committee Wednesday in a contentious six-hour hearing defending their cities' sanctuary policies. The mayors described their approaches, which limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, as humane efforts that reduce crime and build trust with immigrant communities. House Republicans aggressively challenged them, accusing the mayors of harboring dangerous criminals and violating the Constitution. Some lawmakers threatened criminal prosecution and suggested cutting federal funding to sanctuary cities.

The hearing reflected broader tensions over President Trump's immigration enforcement plans and mass deportation efforts. The administration has already sued Chicago over its sanctuary law and threatened to withhold federal funding from such jurisdictions. Republicans praised Trump's approach to border security, while Democrats and the mayors argued their policies don't impede federal enforcement but simply don't devote local resources to it.

New York Mayor Eric Adams faced unique scrutiny given his recent corruption indictment, which the Justice Department moved to dismiss. Democrats questioned whether Adams made agreements with the Trump administration, which he denied. Legal experts suggested the hearing was unlikely to resolve the standoff between cities and federal authorities.

title: Bill nullifying D.C.’s ‘sanctuary city’ law advanced by House Republicans
summary:
A House committee advanced legislation Tuesday targeting Washington, D.C.'s sanctuary city policies, requiring the District to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. The bill, introduced by Representative Clay Higgins of Louisiana, passed on a party-line vote and would effectively nullify a 2019 D.C. law limiting local cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The legislation mandates compliance with ICE detainer requests and information sharing, though it includes an exception for crime victims and witnesses.

The measure still requires approval from the full House and Senate, where it may face filibuster challenges. The action reflects mounting pressure on D.C. from the Republican-controlled Congress, which has constitutional authority to override District policies. Mayor Muriel Bowser has recently adopted a more cautious stance on immigration policy, no longer using the term "sanctuary city," contrasting with her position during President Trump's first term.

D.C. Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton criticized the bill's victim exception as inadequate, while immigrant rights advocates warned it would deter undocumented residents from seeking police assistance. The legislation comes amid broader congressional actions affecting D.C., including a spending bill that officials say cuts over one billion dollars from the District's local budget.

title: US Court says "metering" policy limiting asylum applications is illegal
summary:
A divided U.S. appeals court ruled Wednesday that the federal government's former "metering" policy at the U.S.-Mexico border violated federal immigration law. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals decided 2-1 that border agents must inspect all asylum seekers who arrive at designated border crossings, even if they have not physically crossed into the United States. The metering policy, which turned away migrants once daily asylum application caps were met, was implemented by U.S. Customs and Border Protection in 2016 and rescinded in 2021.

The court affirmed a lower court's decision preventing a 2019 rule limiting asylum eligibility from being applied to migrants previously turned away under metering. Circuit Judge Michelle Friedland wrote that a noncitizen presenting themselves to a border official at a port of entry has arrived in the United States regardless of their exact physical location. The Biden administration had argued that immigration law only applies once migrants enter U.S. territory.

The lawsuit was brought by advocacy group Al Otro Lado and affected migrants in 2017. In dissent, Circuit Judge Ryan Nelson argued that arrival requires physical presence in the country, calling the majority's interpretation "wrong, troubling, and breathtaking."

title: How Biden's order restricting asylum claims actually works
summary: President Joe Biden announced Tuesday a halt to asylum processing at the U.S.-Mexico border when illegal entries exceed 2,500 daily arrests. The measure took effect immediately, as approximately 4,000 people are currently entering daily. This represents a significant policy shift on a critical election-year issue that has exposed Biden to Republican criticism. Advocates warn the measure endangers migrants and violates international obligations, though the administration disputes this. Legal challenges are expected, and questions remain about the policy's effectiveness. Mexico has agreed to accept returned migrants, but only in limited numbers, and the U.S. lacks sufficient funding and diplomatic support for long-distance deportations to countries like China and African nations. The asylum halt will continue until daily arrests fall below 1,500 for seven consecutive days, last seen in July 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Migrants denied asylum will face deportation orders, criminal prosecution for repeat attempts, and multi-year bans from legal entry. This follows previous unsuccessful deterrence measures under both Biden and Trump administrations, with similar restrictions implemented in May 2023 showing limited lasting impact.

title: Detention and that border "shutdown": What's really in Biden's bipartisan immigration deal
summary:
A bipartisan border security deal combining $20 billion in emergency spending with significant policy changes faces uncertain prospects despite backing from President Biden, who calls it the "toughest and fairest" immigration bill in decades. The 370-page, $118 billion package, which includes aid to Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan, faces opposition from House Republican leaders, conservative senators, and progressive Democrats who criticize it as either insufficient or too restrictive.

Key provisions include mandatory border shutdowns when illegal crossings exceed 5,000 daily on average or 8,500 in a single day, with reopening only when encounters drop to 75 percent of closure levels. The measure aims to expedite asylum processing to six months, requiring stronger proof from applicants while providing legal representation. Immigration and Customs Enforcement would receive nearly $8 billion, including $3 billion for detention capacity, while Customs and Border Protection would get $7 billion for hiring and operations.

The bill allocates 250,000 new visas over five years, offers permanent residency to Afghan allies, provides work authorization for certain visa holders' families, and includes $48 million for anti-fentanyl efforts. It also mandates construction of Trump-era border barriers and provides pathways to citizenship for "Documented Dreamers."

title: Trump cuts exacerbate budget fights in red states
summary:
Republican-led states are confronting significant budget challenges in 2026, partly due to President Donald Trump's tax and spending legislation. The federal tax cuts and new Medicaid and SNAP requirements are costing some states up to $450 million annually in additional expenses and reduced tax revenue. State legislatures are now considering various cuts, including child care subsidies in Missouri, five percent reductions across Arizona state agencies, and $22 million from Idaho disability services.

Many states automatically align their tax codes with federal cuts, resulting in decreased state revenue. However, some Republican states are selectively declining certain provisions. Nebraska rejected tax cuts on tips and overtime, while Idaho opted out of specific corporate tax changes. Indiana's temporary adoption of federal tip and overtime tax cuts is projected to cost $251 million in 2026, while Arizona could lose $381 million.

The legislation also requires states to fund new Medicaid work requirements and SNAP administrative improvements. States face penalties for inaccurate SNAP payments if they don't invest in technology and staffing. These budget pressures are compounded by preexisting deficits from expired Covid-era relief funds and previous state-level tax cuts.

title: Republicans lay groundwork for "total tax cliff" at end of Trump's term
summary:
Congressional Republicans are establishing a potential tax cliff at the end of President Trump's second term by proposing to make 2017 tax cuts permanent while allowing newer provisions to expire in 2028. The House-passed bill includes temporary measures such as increased standard deductions, enhanced child tax credits, and elimination of taxes on tips, overtime pay, and car loan interest. These expiring provisions total approximately $1.5 trillion in tax breaks. Critics, including Representative Chip Roy, characterize this approach as a budgetary gimmick similar to the current situation with expiring 2017 tax cuts.

Senate Republicans appear receptive to maintaining the distinction between permanent and temporary cuts, prioritizing permanence for the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act while remaining flexible on newer provisions. Many policy experts from both political perspectives view Trump's campaign-trail tax proposals as poor policy. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the House bill would add $3 trillion to deficits over ten years when including interest costs, while projecting minimal economic growth of 0.03 percent. Democrats argue the legislation favors wealthy Americans, noting that half of one major deduction went to the top one percent of taxpayers in 2022.

title: Can Trump's tax cuts be made permanent? Tariffs, spending fights cloud the picture
summary: Republican efforts to permanently extend President Donald Trump's 2017 tax cuts face significant obstacles as lawmakers disagree on funding mechanisms amid concerns about economic growth. With an unofficial House deadline approximately two weeks away, party members are divided over whether the expiring Tax Cuts and Jobs Act provisions can be made permanent without substantially increasing the $36 trillion national debt and $1.9 trillion annual deficit. Moderate Republicans oppose large Medicaid cuts needed to achieve $2 trillion in offsetting spending reductions, while hardliners demand scaling back tax cuts if savings targets cannot be met. Republican leadership projects the cuts will generate sustained 2.6% GDP growth, adding $2.5 trillion in revenue over ten years. However, budget analysts consider these forecasts overly optimistic, particularly given Trump's trade policies and immigration crackdown, which may constrain economic expansion. The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget found the 2017 tax cuts added approximately $1.9 trillion to national debt. Some estimates suggest Trump's broader tax proposals could cost up to $6 trillion over a decade. Democrats criticize the Republican agenda as fiscally irresponsible and harmful to government program beneficiaries.

title: US Senate plan to make Trump tax cuts permanent raises "debt spiral" worry
summary: U.S. Senate Republicans are pursuing a controversial plan to make President Donald Trump's 2017 tax cuts permanent through a parliamentary maneuver that would bypass Democratic opposition by ignoring projected revenue losses exceeding $4 trillion. The strategy involves claiming tax policy would remain unchanged to circumvent rules prohibiting bills from expanding the deficit beyond ten years. The proposal faces opposition from Republican fiscal conservatives who hold crucial votes in the narrowly divided House, where Republicans maintain only a 218-215 majority. Representatives Thomas Massie, Victoria Spartz, and David Schweikert have expressed concerns that the plan avoids difficult decisions on spending cuts. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget warns the permanent tax cuts could trigger a debt spiral, potentially adding $4.6 trillion to deficits over the next decade. While the Congressional Budget Office estimated the 2017 tax cuts increased the deficit by nearly $1.9 trillion over ten years, Republicans argue economic growth will offset costs. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other Republicans must craft legislation that can pass both chambers while facing upcoming deadlines on government funding and raising the debt ceiling.

title: US Senate Republicans pass measure to move forward on Trump's tax cuts
summary:
The U.S. Senate approved a Republican budget blueprint early Saturday by a 51-48 vote, aiming to extend President Donald Trump's 2017 tax cuts and reduce government spending. The measure enables budget reconciliation, allowing Republicans to bypass the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold and advance Trump's tax, border security, and military priorities without Democratic support. Two Republicans, Senators Susan Collins and Rand Paul, joined Democrats in opposition.

The blueprint now moves to the Republican-controlled House of Representatives for consideration next week. Non-partisan analysts estimate the Trump agenda would add approximately $5.7 trillion to federal debt over ten years, though Senate Republicans claim the cost is $1.5 trillion, arguing that extending existing tax policy should not count toward the measure's cost. The plan also seeks to raise the debt ceiling by $5 trillion and offset tax cut costs through spending reductions.

Democrats warned that Republican spending targets could threaten Medicaid and other social programs. The vote occurred amid significant stock market volatility following Trump's new trade tariffs. During debate, Republicans added provisions to protect Medicaid and Medicare while rejecting numerous Democratic amendments aimed at safeguarding various government assistance programs.

title: Trump tax bill averts one debt crisis but makes future financial woes worse
summary:
Congress passed President Donald Trump's tax-cut and spending bill on Thursday, averting an immediate government default while worsening America's long-term debt situation. The legislation extends Trump's 2017 tax cuts, increases spending on border security and the military, and cuts Medicare and Medicaid. It raises the government's $36.1 trillion borrowing limit by $5 trillion, eliminating concerns about a potential default that could have occurred in late August or early September.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates the bill will add $3.4 trillion to national debt over the next decade, reducing tax revenues by $4.5 trillion while cutting spending by $1.2 trillion. Approximately 10.9 million people are projected to lose federal health insurance. Investment firms including BlackRock have warned that foreign buyers are losing interest in American debt, with ongoing fiscal deficits and elevated debt levels raising concerns about Treasury demand and borrowing costs.

While some analysts predict the bill could boost economic growth by up to 0.5 percent next year, others worry about long-term risks of higher borrowing costs. Market reaction has been relatively muted, with investors focusing primarily on earnings reports and Federal Reserve policy decisions.

title: What need to know about the child tax credit as both campaigns embrace it
summary: Republican Vice Presidential candidate JD Vance proposed increasing the child tax credit to $5,000 per child for all American families regardless of income. Vice President Kamala Harris announced plans to restore the COVID-era policy and provide a $6,000 tax credit for families with newborn babies in their first year. The child tax credit has existed for over 25 years, currently providing eligible families up to $2,000 per child. In 2021, the American Rescue Plan Act temporarily expanded the credit to $3,600 per child annually, made it available to low-income families regardless of tax liability, and distributed it monthly. This expansion cut child poverty rates in half and helped 19 million additional children qualify. When the expanded credit expired, poverty rates increased again. Research indicates the expansion improved child health and well-being, particularly for poor children. Congress recently failed to pass a child tax credit expansion after some Republican senators opposed it. Experts note the policy has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, though details matter significantly. Economists emphasize that targeting low-income families produces the greatest benefits for child welfare.

title: Measuring the cost of extending Trump's tax cuts becomes a flashpoint in Congress
summary:
Senate Republicans are seeking to change how the extension of President Trump's 2017 tax cuts would be calculated regarding future federal deficits. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that extending these cuts would increase deficits by nearly $4 trillion over ten years. Republicans propose using a baseline that assumes the tax cuts will continue regardless of expiration dates, effectively treating their renewal as cost-free. This approach would allow them to pass legislation with a simple majority rather than the typical 60-vote threshold required to overcome a filibuster.

Democrats accuse Republicans of violating Senate norms by bypassing the Senate parliamentarian's ruling on whether this scoring change complies with budget reconciliation rules. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer characterized the move as "going nuclear" on institutional rules. Business groups support the change, arguing it provides economic certainty, while fiscal watchdog organizations warn it represents an accounting gimmick that obscures the true cost and sets a dangerous precedent. House Republicans have taken a different approach, acknowledging the costs and proposing spending cuts to offset them. Critics warn this precedent could enable future Democratic majorities to make new spending programs permanent through similar methods.

title: How Trump's megabill transfers wealth in the US
summary:
House Republicans passed a comprehensive tax and spending bill this week after intense lobbying from President Donald Trump. The legislation extends tax cuts from Trump's first term while reducing spending on Medicaid and food assistance programs. According to Congressional Budget Office estimates, the package would increase the deficit by $3.8 trillion over ten years through tax measures, while cutting nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid and food stamps. Medicaid would face approximately $700 billion in reductions, and SNAP would see $267 billion in cuts. Overall, the bill would add $3.1 trillion to the national debt over the next decade.

Analysis from the Tax Policy Center shows that over 80% of Americans would receive tax cuts compared to current law, averaging $2,900 per household. However, 60% of tax benefits would go to the top 20% of earners. The Penn Wharton Budget Model found that when accounting for both tax cuts and spending reductions, the lowest-income Americans would see their incomes fall by an average of $820, while highest earners would gain over $12,000. The bill now moves to the Senate, where modifications are expected.

title: Investors see worsening US deficit outlook as tax bill heads to Senate
summary:
Investors are concerned that a sweeping tax and spending bill moving through the Senate could worsen U.S. debt projections and keep bond yields elevated. The House version of the bill is projected to add approximately $3.8 trillion to the federal government's $36.2 trillion debt over the next decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Markets have been sensitive to deteriorating U.S. debt conditions, particularly following Moody's downgrade of the U.S. sovereign credit rating in May. Long-dated bonds have been especially affected, with the 30-year bond yield reaching its highest level since October 2023.

Analysts anticipate that as the bill progresses through the Senate, spending cuts may be reduced while stimulus measures could be added, potentially increasing the deficit further. President Trump has requested a final bill by July 4. The White House emphasizes $1.6 trillion in spending cuts and argues that tax cuts will generate $2.5 trillion in new revenue through economic growth. Some investors express disappointment with the bill's current form, having expected more substantial spending reductions. Despite concerns, certain investors view the higher yields on longer-term bonds as attractive opportunities.

title: GOP Lawmakers appear skeptical of Trump's $2,000 tariff rebate checks
summary: President Trump has proposed $2,000 payments to low- and middle-income households funded by tariff revenue, but the plan faces significant resistance from Republican lawmakers. GOP members of Congress express reluctance to approve such checks, preferring instead to use tariff revenue to reduce budget deficits or fund healthcare initiatives addressing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies. The proposal recalls Trump's first-term stimulus payments during the coronavirus pandemic, which he hopes will boost Republican prospects before the 2022 midterm elections. However, Republicans and economists worry the payments could fuel inflation similar to what occurred after Biden-era stimulus checks. According to the Tax Foundation, Trump's tariffs are expected to generate $158 billion in 2025 and $2.3 trillion over ten years, while targeted $2,000 payments could cost between $280 billion and $607 billion depending on structure. The administration has presented conflicting messages about tariff revenue usage, and lawmakers report receiving no detailed proposals. While the White House claims it has sufficient votes for approval, most Republican legislators remain skeptical, citing concerns about the $1.8 trillion budget deficit. Senator Josh Hawley represents a notable exception, having introduced legislation for tariff rebate checks.

title: Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill" heads to senate, where new fights loom
summary:
President Trump's legislative package narrowly passed the House early Thursday morning by a single vote after an overnight session, and now faces uncertain prospects in the Senate. The 1,000-page bill extends expiring tax cuts, eliminates taxes on tips, overtime pay, and Social Security benefits, and increases funding for border security and the military while cutting Medicaid, food aid, and higher education programs. The legislation is projected to add $2.7 trillion to budget deficits through 2034.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune must navigate competing demands within his narrow Republican majority. Some senators seek deeper spending cuts, particularly to Medicaid, while others want permanent tax cuts or gentler phaseouts of clean-energy incentives. The House provision raising the state and local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000 faces Senate opposition. Senators Rand Paul and Ron Johnson have already expressed strong reservations about the bill.

House Speaker Mike Johnson warned against major Senate changes that could unravel the fragile House coalition. Any Senate modifications must return to the House for approval before reaching Trump's desk, with Republicans targeting a July 4 deadline for completion.

title: Senate kills bipartisan tax bill
