summary: A bipartisan tax bill that passed the House with overwhelming support failed to advance in the Senate on Thursday, falling short of the 60 votes needed to proceed. The nearly $80 billion legislation would have revived expired business tax provisions for capital investments and research, expanded the low-income housing tax credit and child tax credit for low-income families, and terminated the fraud-plagued employee-retention tax credit from the pandemic era. The bill received support from both progressive antipoverty organizations and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The Senate vote resulted in 48 in favor and 44 against, with most Republicans opposing the measure, arguing it favored Democratic priorities and made the child tax credit too generous for parents without earnings. Some Republicans suggested they could craft better legislation if they gain more control after November's election. Three Senate Republicans voted yes, while two Democratic caucus members, including Bernie Sanders, voted no. The bill's failure leaves business owners facing higher tax bills due to changes in research expense deductions, with some warning of potential layoffs. Democrats plan to use the vote as a campaign issue, particularly highlighting Republican opposition to family tax benefits.

title: Republicans and democrats prepare for a tax-policy fight
summary:
The US economy added 272,000 jobs in May, significantly exceeding economist expectations, while average hourly wages rose and unemployment ticked up to 4% for the first time in over two years. The strong jobs report suggests the Federal Reserve may delay interest rate cuts as it continues efforts to control inflation. Major stock indexes posted slight declines but logged weekly gains to start June.

GameStop announced first-quarter earnings showing a narrowed loss and declining sales, along with plans to offer 75 million shares. Meme stock investor Keith Gill, known as "Roaring Kitty," livestreamed for the first time in nearly three years, revealing he still holds his GameStop position. The stock fell 40% during his appearance, with trading halted 16 times.

Tax cuts from the 2017 Trump administration law are set to expire at the end of 2025, creating a policy battle between Republicans and Democrats. The law permanently reduced corporate tax rates from 35% to 21% and temporarily lowered individual tax rates and increased deductions. Republicans favor extending all cuts, while Democrats want to maintain cuts only for those earning under $400,000 while raising taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals.

title: House passes $78B tax bill in rare bipartisan vote
summary:
The House passed a $78 billion bipartisan tax package Wednesday evening by a vote of 357 to 70, combining an expansion of the Child Tax Credit with several business tax breaks. The legislation now moves to the Senate, where it faces an uncertain future as some Republican senators call for hearings and modifications.

The bill pairs Democratic priorities, including expanded child tax credits benefiting an estimated 16 million children and potentially lifting 400,000 out of poverty, with Republican-sought business tax cuts. These include restored immediate deductions for research and development costs, relief for companies in the U.S. and Taiwan, and increased affordable housing tax credits.

Opposition came from both extremes: House progressives argued the package insufficiently addresses child poverty, while conservative Republicans criticized it as welfare expansion, particularly objecting to refundable credits potentially reaching undocumented immigrants with U.S.-born children.

The passage represents a significant achievement for Speaker Mike Johnson and demonstrates rare bipartisan cooperation in a typically gridlocked Congress. The legislation was crafted by House Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith and Senate Finance Committee Chair Ron Wyden. The Senate is unlikely to consider the package until March due to other priorities, including government funding bills.
